opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly, from the outside it can look like I've been jumping around between very different domains. But to me there's a single thread that runs through all of it, and that thread is networks, or more generally, relational structure.

When I started out, I was studying online social networks and human behavior: how information spreads, how people form communities, how influence works. What struck me early on was that you can't understand an individual's behavior in isolation. You have to understand who they're connected to and how those connections shape what they do. The signal is in the relationships.

Then when we moved into biology, it turned out to be exactly the same story, just with different nodes and edges. Proteins interact with other proteins, genes regulate other genes, drugs bind to targets, diseases share molecular pathways. If you look at a single protein, you learn a little. If you look at its neighborhood in the interaction network, you learn a lot more. That's what drove a lot of our work on graph neural networks: we needed machine learning methods that could natively learn from that kind of interconnected structure instead of forcing everything into flat feature vectors.

And the enterprise piece is, in some sense, the most practical realization of that same idea. If you look at how companies actually store their data, it's in relational databases: customers, transactions, products, events, all in different tables linked by primary and foreign keys. That's a graph. It's a heterogeneous, temporal graph. But the way the industry has done machine learning on it for decades is to have data scientists manually join tables and hand-engineer features, flattening all that rich structure into one big table before they can train a model. It's slow, it's brittle, and you throw away a lot of signal.

So the insight we had was: why not treat the relational database as a graph directly and learn on it end-to-end? That's what we've called relational deep learning. You take the tables, turn rows into nodes and key relationships into edges, and let a graph neural network, or now a graph transformer or foundation model, learn the representations automatically. And it turns out the same principles that help you predict which proteins interact or how a social behavior spreads also help you predict customer churn, fraud, or what someone will buy next.

So, social networks, biological networks, enterprise data: different surfaces, but underneath it's all about learning from relationships. And I think the big lesson across all of it is that the most valuable information is often not in the individual data points but in how they connect.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so it may look like three completely different things, but for me there's really one thread running through all of it, and that thread is relationships. The way I think about it is that the interesting stuff in the world is almost never about an individual object in isolation. It's about how things connect to each other.

So if you look at human behavior, which is where I started, with social networks and online communities and information spreading, the whole point is that people don't act independently. What I do depends on what my friends do, what I see, who I interact with. You can't understand an individual without understanding the network they're embedded in.

Then when I moved into biology, I realized it's exactly the same picture. A protein doesn't do anything by itself. It interacts with other proteins, it's regulated by genes, it's expressed in certain cell types, it's affected by drugs. Disease is really a network phenomenon. So the graph is there, it's just that the nodes are now molecules and cells instead of people.

And the enterprise setting, which is what I've been spending a lot of time on recently with Kumo, is actually the most explicit version of this. Every company stores its data in relational databases. You have a customers table, a transactions table, a products table, and they're connected by keys. That is literally a graph. People just don't usually think of it that way, because they've been trained to flatten it into a single table with a bunch of hand-engineered features before they do any machine learning.

So the connection, from my point of view, is that all three are instances of the same underlying problem: learning from relational, networked data. And that's why graph neural networks and now relational foundation models have been so central to my group's work. The same machinery that helps you predict which drug will interact with which protein can help you predict which customer is going to churn next month. The domain changes, but the structure of the problem, and the methods you need to attack it, are remarkably consistent.

astra-6.text:
The common thread is relationships. Whether you’re studying human behavior, biology, or enterprise data, you have entities that interact, and understanding those interactions is often essential to understanding the system.

For human behavior, that might mean looking at how people connect and influence one another. In biology, you might have proteins interacting with other proteins, and you want to understand how those interactions relate to a disease. In an enterprise, you have customers, products, and transactions distributed across connected tables.

These look like very different domains, but they share a computational question: How do we learn from the structure of those relationships? A graph gives us a way to represent that structure, and machine learning lets us use it to make predictions. What’s exciting to me is that we can develop methods around that shared structure while still respecting what makes each domain different.

sol-6.1.text:
The connection is really the relationships. In human behavior, we might study how people connect to one another and how information spreads through those connections. In biology, we have proteins or genes interacting with one another. And in an enterprise, we have customers, products, transactions, and all the relationships between them.

These look like very different domains, but from a computational perspective, they share a structure: you have entities, you have connections, and you want to understand how those connections shape what happens. A customer’s behavior, for example, is better understood in the context of what they’ve purchased and how those products relate to other products.

So the common thread in my work is to use that relational structure to learn and make predictions. Graphs give us a language for representing it, and machine learning gives us tools for extracting useful patterns from it. The scientific questions differ, but many of the underlying computational ideas carry across these settings.
